Vocabulary
A Cosmology Lesson · Grades 5 to 7

The Story of Everything

From the first tiny moment to galaxies, planets, and the strange question of whether there are other universes.

Scroll to begin
01 One Big Number

13.8 billion years ago, the universe was a single, tiny, blazing-hot point.

Then it grew. Not into space. It grew space itself.

That word, cosmology, comes from a Greek word for "the world order." It is the science of the whole universe at once.

This lesson is the short version of a 13.8 billion year story. We will move from the first instant, through the first light, into galaxies, planets, and finally to a few weird ideas that scientists are still arguing about.

Keep an eye out for gold underlined words. Tap any of them for a definition.

02 Common Mistake

It was not an explosion.

People say "the Big Bang" and picture a giant bomb going off in a dark room. That picture is wrong.

A bomb explodes inside a room that already exists. The Big Bang was different. There was no room around it. There was no "outside." Every part of the universe was once squeezed together. Then space itself stretched.

Notice something strange. From any raisin, every other raisin is moving away. There is no "center" raisin where the whole thing started. The dough is stretching everywhere at once.

The universe is doing the same thing right now. Distant galaxies are moving away from us. The farther away they are, the faster they seem to go. That is how we know space is still expanding.

Quick Check
Why is the raisin bread a better picture than a regular explosion?
03 The Timeline

The whole story, in eight steps.

Scroll. Each step changes the picture. Each step also changes the clock.

The early universe moved fast. The clock starts in tiny fractions of a second. By the bottom of this section, you will be looking at the universe today, 13.8 billion years later.

10⁻³² seconds · Inflation
1 microsecond · First Particles
3 minutes · First Nuclei
380,000 years · First Light
200 million years · First Stars
400 million years · Galaxies Form
10 billion years · Dark Energy Wakes Up
13.8 billion years · Today
10⁻³² seconds

Inflation

Almost the moment time began, the universe stretched faster than you can imagine. In a tiny fraction of a second, it may have grown by a factor of ten followed by thirty zeros.

This is called inflation. During inflation, space itself stretched. This is not the same as objects flying through space.

1 microsecond

The First Particles

One millionth of a second after the Big Bang, the universe was a hot soup of tiny particles. Protons, neutrons, and electrons all formed in this messy plasma. Light was constantly bouncing off everything.

If you had been there, you would not have been able to see your hand in front of your face.

3 minutes

The First Nuclei

Three minutes is faster than it takes to microwave a burrito. But in that time, the universe had cooled enough for protons and neutrons to stick together into the cores of the first atoms.

Almost all of the universe's hydrogen and helium was made in this short window.

380,000 years

The First Light

The universe finally cooled enough for electrons to settle around nuclei and form real atoms. Suddenly, light could travel freely. The cosmic fog cleared.

That ancient light is still around. We call it the cosmic microwave background. It is the oldest thing we can see.

200 million years

The First Stars

For a long time, the universe was full of atoms but had no stars. Gravity quietly pulled gas into denser clumps.

Then the first stars switched on. NASA thinks these earliest stars were 30 to 300 times the mass of our Sun and millions of times brighter. They lived fast and exploded young.

400 million years

Galaxies Form

Stars do not float alone. They gather. Pulled together by gravity and shaped by mysterious dark matter, the first galaxies took shape. They were smaller and messier than today's galaxies.

10 billion years

Dark Energy Speeds Things Up

For a long time, gravity slowed the universe's expansion. Then something flipped. About nine billion years after the Big Bang, expansion started to accelerate.

Scientists call the cause dark energy, but that is mostly a placeholder name. Nobody knows what it really is.

13.8 billion years

Today

The universe is enormous, structured, and still expanding faster than ever. There are spiral galaxies, planets, oceans, and creatures who can study the universe they came from.

That last part is us.

04 The Universe's Baby Picture

This is the oldest light you will ever see.

About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe became transparent for the first time. The light from that moment is still racing around. We can detect it. We can map it.

It looks like static, but every dot tells a story. The orange spots are slightly warmer. The blue spots are slightly cooler. Those tiny differences are like baby footprints. They show where matter was a little more bunched up than average. Over billions of years, those bunched-up spots became stars, galaxies, and us.

The whole map is only a few degrees above absolute zero. Cold, faint, ancient. But it is everywhere, in every direction you look.

Worth knowing

When you tune an old TV to a channel that has nothing on it and see static, a tiny bit of that static is actually the cosmic microwave background. You are literally watching the early universe.

05 Galaxies

Stars do not float alone. They gather.

A galaxy is a giant city of stars, gas, dust, dark matter, and often a supermassive black hole at the center.

Our galaxy is the Milky Way. It is a barred spiral, which means it has spiral arms and a stretched bar through the middle. The Sun sits in a smaller branch called the Orion Arm, far from the center.

Galaxies come in a few main shapes.

⊙

Elliptical

Smooth, round or oval blobs of mostly older stars. Not much new star making.

✺

Spiral

Flat disks with curved arms. Full of gas, dust, and bright young stars. The Milky Way is one.

⌬

Barred Spiral

Spirals with a bar of stars cutting across the middle. Our galaxy is actually this kind.

⌇

Irregular

Galaxies that lost their shape, often because gravity from a nearby galaxy pulled them apart.

In a single deep photo from the Hubble Space Telescope, you can count hundreds of galaxies. Each one of those tiny smudges contains billions of stars.

Quick Check
What shape is the Milky Way?
06 Clusters and Lensing

Galaxies gather too.

Just like stars do not float alone, galaxies don't either. They form groups, and groups join into galaxy clusters.

The Milky Way is part of a small gathering called the Local Group, which includes the Andromeda galaxy and dozens of smaller galaxies. The Local Group itself is part of a much larger structure called the Laniakea Supercluster.

Galaxy clusters are so massive that their gravity actually bends light. Light from a galaxy behind a cluster gets deflected on its way to us, and the cluster acts like a giant natural lens.

This effect is called gravitational lensing, and it lets astronomers see distant objects that would otherwise be invisible.

07 The Cosmic Web

Zoom out far enough, and the universe looks like a web.

Galaxies do not spread out evenly. They line up along long threads called filaments. Where filaments meet, clusters form. Between the threads, there are enormous empty regions called voids.

A useful way to picture it: imagine soap bubbles stuck together.

The galaxies live on the thin walls between the bubbles. The insides are mostly empty. The whole pattern is called the cosmic web.

This pattern is not random. It grew over billions of years from those tiny temperature wobbles you saw in the cosmic microwave background map. Slightly denser spots pulled in more matter. Less dense spots emptied out. Given enough time, gravity carved the universe into this web.

08 You Are Here

Earth is not the center.

We are on a small planet, orbiting an ordinary star, in one arm of one galaxy, in one supercluster, on one filament of the cosmic web.

The upper estimate for the number of galaxies in the universe is around two trillion. Each one has hundreds of billions of stars. Many of those stars have planets.

This is not meant to make you feel small. It is meant to give you a sense of how much stuff there is, and how much of it scientists have figured out, just by carefully measuring light.

Quick Check
Roughly how many galaxies do scientists think exist in the observable universe?
09 What Is It All Made Of?

Most of the universe isn't made of stuff you know.

If you scooped up every star, planet, asteroid, person, and bug, you would have only a tiny fraction of the universe's total energy. The rest is two things that nobody really understands.

Dark Matter

Dark matter does not give off light. You cannot see it. But it has gravity. Galaxies spin too fast to hold themselves together with the visible stars alone, so something invisible must be there, adding gravity. That something is dark matter.

The name "dark" just means "we cannot see it directly." It does not mean evil or shadowy. It just means hidden from our usual tools.

Dark Energy

Dark energy is even weirder. About nine billion years after the Big Bang, the universe started expanding faster, not slower. Something is pushing space outward harder than gravity is pulling matter together.

We have no idea what that something is. The honest answer is: this is one of the biggest open questions in science right now.

A useful fact

Ordinary matter, the stuff you can touch, makes up only about five percent of the universe. Dark matter is around twenty-seven percent. Dark energy is the rest. That means more than ninety-five percent of the universe is made of things we cannot directly see or fully explain.

10 Closer to Home

How a star, eight planets, and a dwarf named Pluto got made.

About 4.6 billion years ago, somewhere in the Milky Way, a cloud of gas and dust started to collapse. Most of the cloud fell toward the center and became the Sun. The leftovers flattened into a spinning disk.

That disk is called the solar nebula. Inside it, tiny dust grains started to stick together. Two grains became a clump. Two clumps became a pebble. Pebbles slammed into pebbles and made boulders. Boulders made planetesimals. Eventually you get planets.

This process is called accretion.

The inner part of the disk was hot. Only rocks and metals could survive there. So Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars all turned out small and rocky.

The outer disk was cold. Ice could exist there, and there was way more material. That is why Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune grew huge.

11 The Neighborhood

A quick tour of our solar system.

Eight planets, five officially recognized dwarf planets, hundreds of moons, and millions of asteroids and comets.

★
The Sun

A star. Holds the whole solar system together with its gravity. Most of the mass is here.

Rocky
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars

Small, made of rock and metal. Only Earth has liquid water on its surface and life.

Belt
The Asteroid Belt

A region between Mars and Jupiter filled with rocky leftovers. The dwarf planet Ceres lives there. It is not packed like in movies. Spacecraft pass through it safely.

Giants
Jupiter and Saturn

Gas giants. Mostly hydrogen and helium, like the Sun, but far too small to ever become stars. Saturn has the famous rings.

Icy
Uranus and Neptune

Ice giants. Hydrogen and helium mixed with water, ammonia, and methane. Cold and blue.

12 The Outer Edges

Beyond Neptune, the cold storage zone.

Past Neptune is a flat disk of icy bodies called the Kuiper Belt. This is where Pluto lives. It is also where many of the comets we see come from.

Way, way farther out, possibly thousands of times the distance from Earth to the Sun, is the Oort Cloud. It is a huge bubble of icy objects wrapped all the way around the Sun like a shell.

No one has ever taken a direct picture of the Oort Cloud as a whole. We know it is probably there because of the strange, looping paths of long-period comets. They appear to come from every direction, which suggests they live in a spherical shell, not a flat disk.

A scale fact

An astronomical unit, or AU, is the average distance from Earth to the Sun. The Oort Cloud may stretch from 5,000 AU all the way to 100,000 AU. By comparison, Pluto is only about 40 AU from the Sun. The Oort Cloud is the real edge of our home system.

13 The Family Tree

Zoom out, one step at a time.

Earth's cosmic address has more levels than your mailing address. Each one is much bigger than the last.

Level 1
Planet

Earth. One world, with one Moon.

Level 2
Solar System

The Sun and everything orbiting it. Eight planets, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets.

Level 3
Galaxy

The Milky Way. Hundreds of billions of stars, most with their own planets.

Level 4
Galaxy Group

The Local Group. The Milky Way, Andromeda, and dozens of smaller galaxies bound by gravity.

Level 5
Supercluster

Laniakea. Many galaxy groups and clusters flowing toward a common point.

Level 6
Cosmic Web

The huge filaments, clusters, and voids that make the universe's largest pattern.

Level 7
Observable Universe

Everything we can see. About 93 billion light years across, even though it is only 13.8 billion years old. The expansion of space stretched out the distances.

Earth is not at the center of any of these levels. It is one place among many. That is not bad news. It is just where we happen to live.

14 The Weird Idea

Could there be other universes?

This is the part where we have to be honest. Almost everything in this lesson has solid evidence behind it. The multiverse idea is different. It is interesting. Some of it comes from serious physics. None of it is proven.

There are several versions:

Version 1
More of the same universe

The universe might be much bigger than the part we can see. Beyond our cosmic horizon could be more universe with the same physics. This is the least controversial idea.

Version 2
Bubble universes

Some inflation models suggest inflation never fully stops. Pockets stop and become "bubble universes," while space keeps inflating around them. Each bubble might have different conditions. Possible in some theories, but not confirmed.

Version 3
Many worlds

An idea from quantum physics that says every random quantum event branches reality. Every possible outcome happens, just in different branches. This is debated even among physicists who use it.

Version 4
Different laws

Some highly speculative ideas suggest other universes might have completely different physics. Without a way to test this, it stays in the realm of math and philosophy.

The honest answer is: maybe. We do not know. And we may never be able to test some of these ideas, because by definition they would be outside our universe. That bothers some scientists. Others find it fascinating.

Science vs. story

It is okay to find an idea cool without believing it is proven. Good scientists hold uncertain ideas loosely. Pop science articles often skip that part. Be careful when you see a headline that says "scientists confirm the multiverse." Read the actual paper. Usually it says something more cautious.

15 Confidence Check

Here is what we know well, and what we still don't.

Cosmology is one of the most successful sciences ever. We can measure the age of the universe to within fractions of a percent. But it also has some genuinely unanswered questions.

Strongly supported

  • The universe is expanding
  • The universe was once much hotter and denser
  • The cosmic microwave background exists and comes from the early universe
  • Galaxies formed from tiny early density differences
  • Gravity built the large-scale structure of the universe
  • The solar system formed from a disk of gas and dust about 4.6 billion years ago
  • There are eight planets and many smaller bodies in our solar system

Still uncertain

  • What happened at the very first moment of the universe
  • Exactly how inflation happened, or whether our model is right
  • What dark matter is actually made of
  • What dark energy really is
  • How the first supermassive black holes formed
  • How common life is, or whether we are alone
  • Whether the multiverse is real

"We don't know" is a real scientific answer. It is also where the next discoveries hide.
